_note: Services that turn materials builders already have into what households use: laid walls (shelter is a volume of structure, not a heap of bricks). Each is a recipe on the materials it consumes, so the trades that do the work (mason, carpenter) get labour need from the same household demand that wants the shelter. Every labour figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate of pre-industrial work rates, confidence D, and none is fitted to a target headcount.

brick_wall_m3.basis: per cubic metre of laid brick wall
brick_wall_m3.yield_basis: The bricks are the number that build a cubic metre at the effectiveness data/world/needs.json gives brick_1000 for shelter (1.4 cubic metres of wall per thousand bricks, so 1/1.4 = 0.714 thousand). Mortar joints are about a fifth of a brick wall by volume, at about 1800 kg per cubic metre of lime-sand mortar, so about 360 kg. A bricklayer laid a few hundred bricks in a working day by hand (Trade Warehouse, 'How many bricks can you lay in an hour', https://tradewarehouse.co.uk/blogs/bricks-blog/how-many-bricks-can-you-lay-in-an-hour, opened: 'Experienced professionals can typically lay between 300 to 500 bricks per day', 40 to 60 an hour; taken at the low end, 40 an hour), which is 0.714 * 1000 / 40 = 18 mason hours (was 24 at 30 an hour). LABOURERS (Pass 12, value changed from 18 to 9 labourer hours): Self-Build.co.uk, 'Guide to working with groundworkers and bricklayers' (https://www.self-build.co.uk/guide-working-groundworkers-bricklayers/, opened): 'Bricklayers normally operate in a three-man gang, which is considered the most efficient grouping', 'a single labourer will service two competent brickies', and 'a gang might lay around 1,200 bricks per day', so a half labourer hour per mason hour, 18 * 0.5 = 9 (the old hour-for-hour ratio was 2x above this). The same gang rate is 600 bricks per bricklayer-day, 75 an hour at eight hours, against the 40 an hour here (modern, and a trained bricklayer; the 40 is kept as the slow end for hand-mixed lime mortar and unskilled helpers, within 2x). Order of magnitude only; the rate is the estimate, the quantities are arithmetic. Pass 11 check of the quantities: Wikipedia, Brick (opened) gives the UK standard brick as 215 x 102.5 x 65 mm with a 10 mm joint, a unit cell of 225 x 112.5 x 75 mm (1.9 litres), so a cubic metre of one-brick-thick wall holds about 527 bricks and about 0.27 cubic metres of mortar (arithmetic from those sizes), against 714 bricks and 0.2 cubic metres here: same ballpark (the row counts bricks without their joints). Still unsourced: the roof share below. ROOF: a masonry house is roofed in tile, 100 kg of tile for each cubic metre of wall: about 1.6 square metres of roof a cubic metre of wall (a 5 m by 8 m house with 3 m walls 0.4 m thick) at about 60 kg a square metre; the house shape and the tile weight are ASSUMED, a modern 'Roman' tile is 69 kg a square metre by conversion from a Ludowici product sheet seen in a search summary, not opened (LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D; retire: Complaints/533). Round 4 (Pass 14) roof tile: Ludowici, Roman clay tile product page (https://ludowici.com/product/roman, opened): '1415 lbs.' a square (100 square feet = 9.29 square metres, 240 pieces), so 1415 x 0.4536 / 9.29 = 69 kg per square metre of roof (a modern clay analogue of a Roman tile). Roof area per cubic metre of wall: a 5 m by 8 m house with 3 m walls 0.4 m thick (labelled glue assumptions) has 26 m x 3 m x 0.4 m = 31 m3 of wall and, with a pitched roof taken as 1.2 times its plan area (assumption), 40 x 1.2 = 48 m2 of roof, so 1.55 m2 a cubic metre and 1.55 x 69 = 107 kg of tile, held at 100. All other figures were already sourced above.

stone_wall_m3.basis: per cubic metre of laid dressed-stone wall
stone_wall_m3.yield_basis: Blocks follow the effectiveness data/world/needs.json gives stone_blocks (0.054 cubic metres of wall per block, so 1/0.054 = 18.5 blocks). Ashlar joints are thin, taken as a twentieth of the wall by volume at about 1800 kg per cubic metre, so about 100 kg of mortar. A mason sets a block of about 140 kg (the stone_blocks unit mass) with a gang to lift it, taken as one mason hour per block, and two labourers hoist and bed it: 18.5 mason hours and 37 labourer hours. An estimate of the work rate, confidence D. Pass 11 partial check: Building Construction vol. 4, 'Estimating the Stonework Continued' (https://chestofbooks.com/architecture/Building-Construction-V4/Estimating-the-Stonework-Continued.html, opened, an early twentieth century US manual) estimates ashlar facing at '80 sq. ft. per day for 2 masons and 1 laborer'; for a 0.4 m wall that face rate is about 5 mason hours and 3 laborer hours a cubic metre (arithmetic: 2.5 square metres of face a cubic metre, 7.4 square metres a day for the gang), which is 3.7 times below the 18.5 mason hours here, so the figure is likely high for thin facing and the source does not bound solid ashlar of 140 kg blocks; left unchanged and D. Pass 12 on the labourer count: the same manual says '2 masons and 1 laborer' for ashlar facing, 0.5 labourer per mason, against the 2 labourers per mason here; Self-Build.co.uk (https://www.self-build.co.uk/guide-working-groundworkers-bricklayers/, opened) gives one labourer to two bricklayers for brickwork; no source found for gangs setting 140 kg blocks, where lifting needs more hands, so the 2 per mason is kept as an ASSUMED lifting gang. ROOF: a masonry house is roofed in tile, 100 kg of tile for each cubic metre of wall: about 1.6 square metres of roof a cubic metre of wall (a 5 m by 8 m house with 3 m walls 0.4 m thick) at about 60 kg a square metre; the house shape and the tile weight are ASSUMED, a modern 'Roman' tile is 69 kg a square metre by conversion from a Ludowici product sheet seen in a search summary, not opened (LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D; retire: Complaints/533). Round 4 (Pass 14) roof tile: Ludowici, Roman clay tile product page (https://ludowici.com/product/roman, opened): '1415 lbs.' a square (100 square feet = 9.29 square metres, 240 pieces), so 1415 x 0.4536 / 9.29 = 69 kg per square metre of roof (a modern clay analogue of a Roman tile). Roof area per cubic metre of wall: a 5 m by 8 m house with 3 m walls 0.4 m thick (labelled glue assumptions) has 26 m x 3 m x 0.4 m = 31 m3 of wall and, with a pitched roof taken as 1.2 times its plan area (assumption), 40 x 1.2 = 48 m2 of roof, so 1.55 m2 a cubic metre and 1.55 x 69 = 107 kg of tile, held at 100. Labour: the Building Construction manual's ashlar rate above (80 square feet a day for 2 masons and 1 labourer) is 7.4 mason hours and 3.7 labourer hours a cubic metre for a 0.4 m wall by our arithmetic; the old 18.5 and 37 were 2.5x and 10x above it. Blocks of 140 kg need more hands to lift than facing slabs, so the value is set above the manual's rate and below the old guess: 10 mason hours and one labourer per mason (10 hours; labelled assumption for the lifting gang). Was 18.5 and 37.

timber_frame_m3.basis: per cubic metre of timber in a framed wall or roof, cut, jointed and raised
timber_frame_m3.yield_basis: One cubic metre of timber in the frame is one cubic metre of the structure the shelter need counts (the effectiveness data/world/needs.json gives timber_m3). Hewing to size, cutting joints and raising a frame by hand took a carpenter some tens of hours per cubic metre of timber, taken as 30; labourers help to raise it. An estimate of the work rate, confidence D. NAILS: 2 kg of nails a cubic metre of frame for pegged and nailed joints and boarding (LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found; retire: Complaints/533). SOURCE READ (Pass 8): Mortise and Tenon Magazine, 'The Efficiency of Hewing' (https://www.mortiseandtenonmag.com/blogs/blog/the-efficiency-of-hewing, opened): 'a leisurely 8x8x12' post took around three hours to produce', about 0.15 cubic metres, so hewing alone is about 20 hours a cubic metre; the 30 carpenter hours then leave about 10 for joints and raising, which the source does not bound. Conf D. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: rate from a hewing blog (Mortise and Tenon Magazine, above, 20 hours a cubic metre), a joinery-time search (Fine Homebuilding timber-frame pages and Craftisian, opened via search summaries only, give method but no hours per joint or per bent), and a Roman labour-constants search (DeLaine's Baths of Caracalla appendix; the MDPI and Oxford pages returned 403 and 404). Missing: carpenter hours for joinery and raising per cubic metre of frame.
